item.title: The technology maturity paradox: Why more capabilities can make IT harder
item.description:
Technology maturity is generally considered a sign of progress. Organizations modernize their infrastructure and capabilities, introduce advanced analytics, and invest in AI, all with the expectation that these improvements will make the business more capable, efficient, and competitive.

But there’s a paradox emerging in enterprise IT: The more sophisticated an organization’s technology environment becomes, the more difficult it can be to manage. Every new capability may expand what the business can accomplish while also increasing the number of dependencies, decisions, and stakeholders that must be coordinated. At this rate, technological progress can outpace the organization’s ability to manage it.

As technology portfolios expand, so do the dependencies that IT leaders must understand and coordinate. Recent SoftwareOne research illustrates the disconnect. Although 86% of respondents to a recent survey described their organizations as established, advanced, or highly advanced in their transformation efforts, 41% still identified legacy systems and technical debt as a leading obstacle to execution. Clearly, investing in more advanced technology doesn’t automatically eliminate the challenges that make transformation difficult.

Understand when IT modernization adds complexity

Consider an organization that has invested heavily in Microsoft’s technology ecosystem. Azure supports its cloud infrastructure, Fabric brings together data capabilities, Power BI provides analytics, and Microsoft Foundry enables the development of AI applications and agents.

Individually, each capability may represent an important step forward. But realizing their combined potential requires decisions about how data moves between systems, who governs access, how security policies are enforced, and how new capabilities fit existing business processes.

An AI initiative, for example, may depend on data scattered across legacy databases and cloud environments. Introducing a more sophisticated AI platform won’t resolve inconsistent data definitions, fragmented governance, or architectural limitations that prevent information from being used effectively. In fact, it may make those weaknesses more apparent.

“The hidden cost of adding technology is often the complexity it creates across the organization,” says Michele Carvalho, senior director of Product Development & Readiness at SoftwareOne. “An AI initiative may look successful within one team while exposing gaps in data ownership or governance elsewhere. Intentional IT means looking across the environment before declaring any one deployment a success.”

Rethink what technology maturity means for your enterprise

Traditionally, organizations have measured IT maturity through indicators such as cloud adoption, infrastructure modernization, automation, and the sophistication of their technology capabilities. Those measures remain relevant, but they tell only part of the story. An organization can possess advanced technology and still struggle to integrate systems, manage dependencies, or translate investments into improvements in business performance. Meanwhile, a company with a less sophisticated technology environment may be better positioned to deliver results because its systems, processes, and priorities are more closely coordinated.

This suggests that the next stage of technology maturity may have less to do with the sophistication of individual systems and more to do with the organization’s ability to orchestrate them. Mature IT leadership requires understanding not only what each investment enables, but also how decisions across technology domains and business functions influence one another.

SoftwareOne’s approach to Intentional IT reflects this broader definition of maturity. By looking across software, cloud, data, AI, licensing, security, adoption, and managed services, SoftwareOne helps organizations identify dependencies that might otherwise be overlooked and determine how existing and emerging capabilities can work together more effectively.

For CIOs, the next stage of IT maturity isn’t simply about expanding the technology estate. It’s about building an organization that can navigate the consequences of its investments as the environment evolves. That capability becomes increasingly important as new technologies introduce dependencies that no individual team can manage alone.

“I would ask a different question of a mature IT organization: When priorities change or a new capability emerges, can its teams make a coherent decision together without starting from scratch?” says Carvalho. “That ability to respond with shared context and clear accountability is a stronger sign of progress than the number of platforms deployed.”

Learn how SoftwareOne can help your organization navigate technology decisions with greater clarity and connect investments to business outcomes.

item.title: Why technology is no longer IT’s scarcest resource
item.description:
For much of the history of enterprise IT, technology itself was a limiting factor. Organizations had to make difficult choices about which systems they could afford and which capabilities were realistic to deploy. Technology leaders built their strategies around those constraints.

Today, the challenge looks different. Cloud platforms, advanced analytics, automation, and AI have made sophisticated capabilities accessible to organizations of nearly every size. Microsoft’s expanding portfolio, from Azure and Fabric to Power Platform and Copilot, illustrates just how quickly the range of available options has grown. But greater access to technology has made the job of the tech leader more complicated.

The scarcest resources in IT today are the attention, organizational context, and judgment required to distinguish meaningful opportunities from distractions. The CIO’s challenge is no longer simply understanding what technology can do, but determining what deserves the organization’s finite capacity to act.

Evaluate new capabilities: When opportunity becomes a distraction

Every new capability creates another potential investment decision. AI offers opportunities to improve productivity and automate workflows. Data platforms promise better insights. Cloud modernization can improve scalability and flexibility. Each opportunity may have merit, but pursuing too many simultaneously can stretch resources, introduce complexity, and distract from more pressing business needs.

The temptation to act is particularly strong when technologies are evolving quickly and competitors are announcing ambitious initiatives. But being first to adopt a capability doesn’t necessarily translate into an advantage. Consider Microsoft Copilot. An organization may already have access to the technology through its Microsoft environment, making deployment seem like an obvious next step. But licensing employees for Copilot accomplishes little if the organization hasn’t identified where it can improve work, whether employees are prepared to use it, or how productivity gains will be evaluated. The technology may be ready long before the organization is.

“One of the most consequential decisions a CIO can make is what not to accelerate,” says Michele Carvalho, senior director of Product Development & Readiness at SoftwareOne. “If the organization cannot explain how a new capability will change the work, who will own the outcome and what must be in place first, speed can become a distraction rather than an advantage.”

Prioritize business needs: The value of knowing what to pursue

When technology was scarce, acquiring new capabilities often represented progress. When capabilities are abundant, adding more technology can just as easily create new obligations, dependencies, and costs. An intentional CIO needs to be willing to question the assumption that every promising innovation deserves immediate attention.

That requires a clear understanding of existing investments, business priorities, and organizational capacity. It also means recognizing that the most valuable next move may involve improving adoption of technology already in place, addressing a governance weakness, or reconsidering an initiative whose expected benefits no longer justify its costs.

This is the premise behind SoftwareOne’s approach to Intentional IT: creating the organizational clarity to distinguish between opportunities worth pursuing, investments that require additional groundwork, and capabilities that can wait. Rather than allowing the availability of new technology to dictate priorities, intentional leaders consider how each decision affects the broader technology environment and the business’s capacity to absorb change.

“Intentional IT is not about slowing innovation down,” says Carvalho. “It’s about being deliberate enough to move decisively where the business is ready, and disciplined enough to build the foundation where it is not. The pace of the market must not become the organization’s strategy.”

Learn how SoftwareOne can help your organization navigate technology decisions with greater clarity and connect investments to business outcomes.

item.title: AI datacenter capex will far exceed forecast revenue through 2030
item.description:
Investors are pouring more into AI data center infrastructure than they can hope to recoup by 2030, according to Gartner.

“Enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period,” said Gartner Senior Director Analyst Will Sommer.

AI data center owners would need to generate $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover announced capital spending, financing costs and expected investment returns, he said. “However, total enterprise and consumer AI revenue that can be attributed to AI data centers during this period is forecast to reach no more than $3.6 trillion.”

Gartner joins a growing chorus warning that major AI players may be over-committing themselves. Bain and Co. recently made a similar forecast, estimating that annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion by 2031 and that the AI services market would need to top $6 trillion annually to pay for it.

This is particularly bad news for neocloud providers, said Gartner. While the hyperscalers are large enough to absorb the financial pressures, the research company suggests that the cost pressure will force more than 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations.​

The Bain and Gartner surveys don’t cover quite the same ground, but their conclusions are very similar: a lot of AI infrastructure investment is never going to make a return, and companies need to prepare themselves for some degree of financial loss.

This article first appeared on Network World.

item.title: Change saturation is not a communication problem
item.description:
On a major S/4HANA transformation, the first signs of trouble did not look like resistance. They looked like missed stand-ups. Then deliverables started slipping, readiness checkpoints came back with gaps and the same functional leads kept surfacing on the list of competing priorities.

The people behind those signals were not disengaged. They were functional resources supporting the implementation while still doing their day jobs. At the same time, the organization was adopting Agile ways of working, so they were also learning new project roles, Agile ceremonies, Jira, new testing expectations and new processes. Many of them held real authority in their day jobs that did not carry over into their transformation roles, which meant they were learning to operate without the standing they normally relied on.

When teams fell behind, the response from leadership was reasonable on its face: more meetings, more follow-ups, more frequent status updates. The intent was to get the program back on track. What I watched happen instead was that the same people responsible for completing the work spent more of their week explaining why the work was behind.

That is the pattern most organizations miss. Change saturation gets diagnosed as a communication gap, and the treatment consumes the capacity the team needs to recover.

What misdiagnosed saturation looks like on the ground

Saturation rarely announces itself in an engagement survey. It shows up first in delivery mechanics, and those signals are easy to read as a discipline or messaging problem.

The first signal is erosion in attendance, not pushback. Stand-ups get missed, ceremonies get shorter and the same names drop off invitations. Nobody is objecting to the transformation. They are triaging their calendars.

The second signal is status work crowding out delivery. When a growing share of a team’s week goes to preparing updates, attending check-ins and answering follow-ups, the program has started paying for visibility with the capacity it needs for execution.

The third is readiness gaps that get labeled as training issues. People who attended the sessions still are not ready, because the sessions competed with everything else on their plate and landed at the wrong moment.

The fourth is easy to overlook on global programs: capacity assumptions that do not match the actual calendar. On more than one program, the roadmap accounted for U.S. holidays and overlooked holidays affecting large portions of the teams in India, South America and other locations. The plan was built on capacity that was never there, and the gap surfaced weeks later as slipped dates.

Taken together, these signals point to the same root cause. The work did not get harder. The load did. Yet each signal is usually treated as a separate performance issue and handled with more oversight.

None of this is unusual. In Prosci’s research on change saturation, 78 percent of respondents said their organizations were nearing, at or past the point of saturation, and people managers and front-line employees carry the heaviest load. Those are the same people a transformation depends on to adopt and operate what it delivers.

Why more communication makes it worse

When a program falls behind, the executive instinct is to increase pressure around the existing dates. Add a working session. Increase the cadence of status reporting. Ask for more frequent communication so leadership can see what is happening.

Every one of those moves is made with good intent, and every one of them draws from the same limited pool of time. The people being asked for more updates are the people who were already stretched. On a program adopting Agile at the same time, the added forums sat on top of stand-ups, planning sessions and retrospectives the teams were still learning to run. Visibility goes up, capacity goes down and the program slips further. It also changes how the team experiences the program. Instead of support, they experience scrutiny, and people already carrying two jobs start to feel that the program mostly adds questions.

There is a line I use with leadership teams when this starts to happen:

When a team is behind, the instinct is often to add oversight. But every additional status meeting takes time away from the work you’re trying to accelerate.

Communication and visibility matter. They do not solve an underlying capacity problem, and sometimes they deepen it. Gartner found that only 32 percent of business leaders said the last change they led achieved healthy adoption by employees, and Gartner has argued that leaders get further by making change routine than by trying to inspire people through it. Saturation is a load problem. Louder or more frequent messages to an overloaded team do not reduce the load.

What actually relieves saturation

The moves that worked on my programs were less about new frameworks and more about giving capacity back.

Adjust the operating model as teams mature. Early go-lives needed frequent stand-ups, heavy training and hands-on support. After teams had been through multiple S/4HANA go-lives and understood the process, we deliberately reduced the cadence. Daily meetings became four days a week and eventually two. Holding on to the early-phase cadence after teams had outgrown it would have been another quiet drain. Reducing meetings on a program that has just slipped feels counterintuitive. It requires leadership to trust the dashboards and the team more than the meeting count.

Protect time when the team is on track. On one program, we kept Mondays and Fridays free of meetings when the work was on schedule. It signaled that the time belonged to the work, and teams used it.

Make upcoming work visible instead of asking for more reporting. Readiness dashboards showed what was coming, and we gave advance notice when phases were changing so people could plan around the shift rather than react to it. The dashboards did the job the extra status meetings were trying to do, without taking anyone out of the work.

Make support available without requiring attendance. Recorded training, multiple sessions and office hours let people get targeted help when they needed it without adding another meeting to everyone’s week.

Understand the change landscape before launching the next initiative. That means surveying employees and listening beyond the executive level to the functional teams who will do the work. Executives tend to see initiatives one at a time. Employees experience their cumulative impact alongside their day jobs. Research highlighted in MIT Sloan Management Review found that employees can realistically absorb one or two major changes a year, while leaders are planning for three or four. A short survey of the functional teams will usually surface collisions a portfolio view misses, because those teams feel every initiative that lands in the same week.

The principle behind all of this is one I come back to on every program: “You can’t ask people to absorb more change without giving them something back.”

For CIOs, change saturation is a portfolio decision, not a communications task. CIOs sit where multiple initiatives converge on the same functional teams, and they are often positioned to see the cumulative load before anyone else does. The decisions that relieve saturation are theirs to shape: what gets sequenced first, what waits, what cadence a mature team actually needs and whether the capacity assumptions behind a roadmap match the real calendar.

One practical test helps. Before approving the next initiative or the next status forum, ask which work the affected teams will stop doing to make room for it. If nobody can answer, the capacity is being borrowed.

The organizations that sustain transformation across multiple waves are not the ones with the best change campaigns. They are the ones that treat capacity as a constraint to be managed with the same discipline they apply to budget and scope.

You can’t communicate people into having more capacity. You can only decide, deliberately, how much change you ask them to carry at once.

item.title: AI won’t kill jobs. Bad team design will
item.description:
In a recent finance training session, an FP&A analyst took the prompting method we had covered twenty minutes earlier and applied it to a monthly variance report spanning four business units. The report normally took one and a half to two hours. It was finished in about two minutes, live, in front of the room. Every leader watching did the same math: if experienced people can work like that, why hire the junior analyst in next year’s budget?

That question sits under most of the early AI jobs story, which has been dominated by fear: fewer junior openings, thinner entry-level ladders and senior employees using AI to absorb work that used to train the next generation.

There is evidence behind that concern. Researchers at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab found that employment among workers aged 22 to 25 had fallen in occupations with high exposure to generative AI. The effect was concentrated in jobs where AI could automate tasks. Employment held up better where companies used AI to support employees.

The companies furthest ahead on AI appear to be doing the opposite, according to recent research from Revelio Labs and Ramp reported by the Financial Times. Among nearly 22,000 U.S. companies, the heaviest AI adopters grew white-collar headcount by 10.2% over two years, with entry-level roles up 12%.

The study does not prove that AI caused the hiring. AI adopters were already larger, more engineering-focused and more likely to be growing, but the findings still matter. Companies making serious investments in AI were expanding their workforces, including their junior ranks. Companies making serious investments in AI were expanding their workforces, including their junior ranks. The difference is team design. AI productivity gains have a shelf life: within a year or two the new pace becomes the baseline, and companies that cut their junior layer to capture those gains will have no one ready to step up.

In my previous CIO article, I argued that successful AI adoption requires companies to change how they operate. Giving employees new tools while leaving existing workflows and decision-making structures in place produces scattered experiments and limited gains. Companies need to give the people closest to the work more authority to test AI, improve processes and teach others what works.

Team design is the next part of that transformation. Once AI changes how work gets done, companies also need to change how teams are built and how employees develop. That includes the junior roles where people gain the experience required to become future managers and specialists.

Cutting junior roles creates a capacity problem

The mistake is easy to make. A company trains its existing staff on AI. Suddenly, experienced employees are 30% to 60% more productive. Junior hires start to look like overhead. For a while, that logic feels rational.

The problem is that this kind of approach has an expiry date. A year or two from now, those productivity gains will be absorbed into the business. The new pace will become normal. Clients will expect more. Internal teams will take on more. Senior employees will be stretched again; except this time there won’t be a trained junior layer underneath them.

The company then has limited choices. It can overwork its experienced staff, compete for expensive external hires or promote people before they are ready. Each option carries a cost.

This is a pipeline problem as much as a hiring problem. Companies cannot produce experienced employees on demand. Judgment develops through repeated exposure to real decisions, feedback and consequences.

Research on AI and customer service offers a clue about how companies can approach this. A study of more than 5,000 support agents found that access to a generative AI assistant increased productivity by 15% on average. Less experienced workers benefited the most. The system helped them apply some of the practices used by higher-performing colleagues.

That finding should interest any leader thinking about early-career development. AI can help junior employees reach competence faster when the tool contains useful organizational knowledge and employees receive guidance on how to use it.

Building teams like multi-agent systems

When we build multi-agent AI systems, we usually build them in a hub-and-spoke model. There’s an orchestrator agent in the middle, then smaller agents handling specific tasks around it. In a marketing function, for example, one agent might handle social media, another might handle SEO, another might handle analytics and another might handle reporting. The user works through the orchestrator, which coordinates the system.

I think this model offers a useful template for team design.

The senior employee acts as the hub, with junior employees and AI agents working as the spokes around them. Instead of simply delegating tasks, that senior person shapes how the work gets done: teaching the AI systems and juniors what good looks like, and helping junior employees build judgment by working inside the same system. The junior employee learns from the AI by seeing how it approaches research, drafting, analysis and problem-solving; the AI improves because the junior is constantly correcting, refining, rejecting and escalating its outputs.

That’s where the training model changes. Historically, juniors learned through repetition, writing the first draft, building the spreadsheet, checking the details, sending the recap and slowly absorbing the standards of the job. AI will take over parts of that repetitive work, but it won’t remove the need for training. It changes where the learning happens: juniors are no longer just learning by doing the task from scratch, they’re learning by directing the task, judging the output and feeding better decisions back into the system.

A junior employee now needs to learn how to question an AI output, spot weak reasoning, understand what a client or stakeholder actually needs, and know when to escalate. This kind of judgment is built like a pilot’s instincts: not by watching someone fly, but by spending time in the cockpit as experienced pilots navigate real decisions.

What companies should hire for now

This changes what hiring managers should look for in junior talent.

Curiosity has always been a crucial quality to look for, but it matters even more now. Juniors need to be willing to learn the tools and understand how AI changes the work. But the stronger signals are emotional intelligence, good interpersonal instincts, discernment, judgment and the ability to explain why they made a decision.

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 supports this broader view of skills. Employers expect AI literacy and technological capability to grow in importance. They also continue to value analytical thinking, curiosity, leadership and social skills. The report found that 77% of surveyed employers planned to upskill workers in response to AI disruption.

That’s also why senior employees need to work differently. Engineers need to spend more time with business teams, so they understand how the company actually operates. Business teams need to spend more time with technical teams so they understand what the tools can and can’t do.

If companies want to keep moving faster, they still need to hire junior talent. But the apprenticeship has changed. Instead of learning by taking repetitive work off someone else’s plate, juniors now join AI-enabled teams where they can see how experienced colleagues think, learn from the systems those colleagues build, and develop judgment through decisions they’re gradually trusted to make. We’re all managers now, some will manage humans, some will manage machines and a select few will build the skills to manage both.

item.title: IT leaders still on the hunt for VMware alternatives
item.description:
Nearly three years after Broadcom purchased VMware, IT leaders still aren’t convinced they will stick with the leading virtualization technology provider over the long term.

Ninety percent of current VMware customer CIOs are considering alternatives to VMware due to higher licensing costs since the Broadcom acquisition, according to a recent survey, with over half saying that Broadcom’s decision to end perpetual license support is a major reason they are evaluating other options.

The survey, commissioned by third-party support vendor Rimini Street, also finds 60% of VMware customers considering multiple-hypervisor strategies, to create more flexible virtualization environments.

Since taking over VMware in late 2023, Broadcom has revamped its pricing models, often leading to cost increases of 50% to 200%. In some cases, customers have reported quotes that would result in price hikes of 1,500%.

Keith Costello, Rimini Street’s EVP and COO, says his company has heard widespread dissatisfaction about the price increases, including the transition from perpetual licenses to a subscription model, as well as the push to adopt VMware Cloud Foundation, an integrated software platform for deploying and managing private and hybrid cloud environments.

“What I’m hearing is that they’re not dissatisfied with the product at all,” he says. “VMware’s customers love their product, but the terms under which VMware is providing alternatives, in terms of migration for their customers, doesn’t work with their timelines, doesn’t work with their economics.”

A VMware spokesman declined to respond to the survey results.

The long road to cost recovery when switching vendors

Widespread dissatisfaction doesn’t necessarily mean IT leaders will abandon VMware, adds Joe Locandro, Rimini Street’s CIO. Alternatives have emerged, but VMware has long been a market leader for virtualization, he notes, and switching to new vendors can be expensive, even considering VMware’s price hikes.

The cost of switching to a new vendor can take three to five years to recover, even when users factor in the price increases, and many CIOs don’t consider the costs of retraining staff in new products and the lost opportunity costs created by a long-term transition to a new vendor with major upfront costs, Locandro says.

“You don’t want to jump from one frying pan to another,” he says. “At the end of the day switching is not a competitive advantage; it’s a bit of the infrastructure and plumbing, and there’s the opportunity cost of investment to other AI initiatives and other things that require capital and expenditure.”

Still, many CIOs want more vendor flexibility and control over their virtualization spending, Costello says.

“One thing clients don’t like, and it’s not unique to VMware software and virtualization capabilities, is that they don’t like being forced into a corner to make a choice,” he adds. “CIOs feel a lack of control over their estate, when, all of a sudden, the price for this big technology that they’ve been relying on for 15 years goes up 3x.”

The survey also finds about two-thirds of IT leaders are considering third-party support for end-of-support versions of VMware’s vSphere virtualization product, a service Rimini Street specializes in.

Rethinking VMware as the default — before renewal removes leverage

While Rimini Street has a huge interest in VMware customers exploring alternatives such as third-party support, other observers of the virtualization market also see broad dissatisfaction with the price increases.

Many CIOs and CFOs have been reevaluating VMware in the wake of Broadcom’s licensing changes, says Thomas Cloud, founder of Vertex CIO Advisory and 48 Technologies and director of IT for an MSP.

But leaving VMware immediately is rarely the right approach, he adds.

“The right answer is to understand which workloads still justify the platform, quantify the real cost of staying, understand the cost and risk of moving, and make the decision before the renewal deadline removes your leverage,” he says. “A VMware renewal should be treated like any other material technology dependency: Understand it before the deadline, quantify the alternatives, and don’t let the renewal date make the decision for you.”

A good approach is to separate the workloads that justify staying on VMware from workloads that can move to other providers, Cloud says. “The biggest mistake I see is treating it as an all-or-nothing migration question,” he adds.

Third-party VMware support can also be a useful bridge, he says. “It can give the company time to avoid making a rushed infrastructure decision simply because a renewal date is approaching,” he explains. “But it should be part of an intentional transition or support strategy, not just a way to postpone the same decision indefinitely.”

In addition to advising clients on potential migrations, Cloud’s organizations are reevaluating their use of VMware as well, he says.

“We’re not looking at it as, ‘VMware is now bad; therefore everything has to move,’” he adds. “We’re looking at where VMware still makes operational and economic sense versus where other platforms such as Hyper-V or Azure may be a better fit going forward. The Broadcom changes have definitely made us more willing to challenge the assumption that VMware should automatically remain the default.”

A defector’s tale

Over at the Swiss National Supercomputing Center, engineers and IT leaders began exploring alternatives to VMware in 2021, before the Broadcom acquisition. The center’s transition to SUSE Virtualization was driven more by technical needs, but the price changes at VMware have reinforced the center’s decision, says Maria Grazia Giuffreda, associate director at the center.

The center is also a big supporter of open-source software, and that philosophy drove the organization to seek alternatives, she adds. The center is opposed to paying for software licenses, she notes.

“Cost always has an impact, because you want to reduce your cost wherever possible,” she says. “You sometimes start looking at alternative solutions for reducing the amount of money that you invest, and licenses are an eternal discussion.”

The new solution has reduced the time the center manages infrastructure by 70%, says Dino Conciatore, a systems engineer at the center.

“When we saw the licensing change, we thought, ‘Oh, we’re so lucky, we never liked closed products,’” he adds.

IT leaders seeking options should check out Networkworld’s “5 alternatives to VMware vSphere virtualization platform” and its deeper look at how enterprises are reevaluating their virtualization strategies.

item.title: The agent-to-agent economy is closer than you think
item.description:
Stripe recently acquired AI routing platform OpenRouter for a reported $7.5 billion, making it one of the largest venture-backed AI startup exits and fintech M&A deals of the year. It’s a blockbuster deal that instantly became one of the most intriguing tech developments to occur this year. Not just because of the dollars involved or the reasons your tech newsfeed or social media timeline insists.

The broader perception seems to be that this is just a standard software developer tooling narrative. Financial analysts and tech enthusiasts would have you believe the main takeaways here are the massive acquisition price and Stripe’s shiny new resource to lower AI token costs. To many, OpenRouter is simply a tech-savvy developer utility that routes basic prompts to inexpensive AI models while setting aside pricey frontier models for complicated reasoning tasks. Others view it as a way to prevent vendor lock-in from cloud ecosystem giants such as AWS Bedrock. But these perspectives are missing the big picture.

From my perspective, it’s clear that this acquisition sends a definitive signal about where the future of digital payments is heading – not just the future of artificial intelligence software. While it won’t happen overnight, agent-to-agent commerce is clearly opening the floodgates to a paradigm where autonomous software agents will serve as fully empowered economic participants that can conduct business on behalf of both individuals and enterprises.

In my line of work, that means we aren’t far away from the time when, for example, an automated car insurance agent can eventually meet, negotiate with, evaluate risk for and sell coverage to another company’s autonomous agent – with the entire exchange happening seamlessly behind the scenes.

From agents that assist to agents that transact

Consider how AI agents operate nowadays versus how they will perform in the near future. Today, agents primarily pass context back and forth across software interfaces. Case in point: A consumer uses a car shopping agent to search vehicle inventory for a new Toyota RAV4; after the consumer chooses the exact vehicle they want, the agent passes the pertinent details – make, model, buyer location and other criteria – to an insurance-quoting agent. In this model, data flows fluidly. Yet the software systems themselves complete no actual financial transaction. The agents aid the user, but human intervention via a checkout process, credit card entry or manual sign-off is needed to finalize the vehicle purchase.

Meta’s recent move to open access for developers to build Muse connectors is proof that this transition from passive assistance to direct execution is already underway. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, OpenClaw and Dots can now leverage simple API connectors to handle browsing and user context in the background. At the same time, e-commerce giants like Shopify are giving agents direct access to checkout, with OpenRouter serving as the critical routing engine sitting right in the middle. This demonstrates that the real secret sauce is in the transaction layer, not just model intelligence.

These developments signify a major leap from agent assistance to direct execution. In the agent-to-agent economy just over the horizon, software agents will actively complete end-to-end transactions without an information handoff hard stop. Instead of multiple agents involved, a single AI agent will be able to buy specialized micro-services from another agent, retrieve proprietary data from secure databases, negotiate contract details using preset operational guidelines and fulfill sophisticated tasks on demand.

Before panic ensues, let me make it clear that this shift doesn’t mean real people, or their jobs, will completely disappear from the loop. This entire ecosystem still requires oversight from human beings, who will be needed to set important goals, define ethical boundaries and enforce regulatory safeguards. The fundamental change underway is that the machine-to-machine layer will be increasingly responsible for the mechanics of commerce, and the minutiae humans find tedious.

Agent-to-agent commerce isn’t just a niche tool or a standalone use case. It’s a new layer of interaction, one that could operate just beneath the surface of many existing business processes and revamp how enterprises negotiate, exchange services and produce revenue.

The infrastructure problem

None of this will be easy. Reconfiguring an economy centered around autonomous software agents presents colossal financial and technical challenges that conventional banking systems weren’t designed to navigate. Comprehending the difficulty ahead requires looking more closely at the basic mechanics of machine-to-machine interactions. For starters, software agents interacting in real time lack built-in trust capabilities. They need instant, verifiable financial settlement to validate that tasks have been finished before they can permit access to data or services. What’s more, the dollar amounts involved in these micro-payments are commonly too tiny to validate invoicing methods or standard payment processing workflows.

And therein lies the rub, and the infrastructure gap laid bare: Existing payment systems simply weren’t built for machine-speed, high-volume micro-transactions. Credit card networks, wire transfers and other traditional payment pathways depend on static batch processing, multi-day settlement windows and high fixed transaction fees. For instance, when an AI agent must make a $0.002 micro-payment to another agent to process a 1,000-token prompt, access a database or perform a targeted computation, waiting two business days for an ACH transfer or forking over a $0.30 credit card processing fee makes the whole interaction economically infeasible.

Of course, this infrastructure problem isn’t happening in a vacuum. Significant tech and digital finance players are working furtively to create machine-native transaction systems. Exhibit A: Fintech innovator Circle is crafting stablecoin payment systems that enable AI agents to send and receive funds in real time without human intervention needed. Exhibit B: Joint initiatives are being developed, like the agentic commerce protocols by Stripe and OpenAI. These and other examples prove that industry movers and shakers acknowledge that empowering machines to safely and instantly transact money represents the next crucial frontier for digital infrastructure.

Viewing Stripe’s acquisition of OpenRouter through this lens totally reframes the deal as not just a straightforward software purchase, but a major step in a multi-pronged infrastructure strategy. Think of OpenRouter as a central dispatch hub that oversees and directs scores of AI agent workloads throughout many different systems. It links developers to legions of AI models across numerous providers. And it carefully assesses every incoming request to pick the best model based on cost, speed and complexity of the task. Stripe, on the other hand, serves as the international financial backbone in this dynamic, providing stablecoin rails and the micro-payment wherewithal necessary for real-time monetary settlement.

Like two gigantic pipes that thread snugly together, Stripe and OpenRouter become the missing plumbing for agent-to-agent commerce. OpenRouter functions as the master control valve in this metaphor, directing where tasks go; Stripe then supplies the high-pressure financial flow that instantly settles the value exchanged.

It’s this synergistic dynamism that helps the estimated $7.5 billion price paid make sense. This isn’t merely an existing software business with a dependable revenue stream Stripe is absorbing; the new parent company is securing a controlling position at the precise historical inflection point where AI workloads pivot to autonomous commerce. Stripe is now strategically placed at the intersection of digital payment settlement and model orchestration. Consequently, as AI agents emerge as primary economic drivers, every token request and micro-transaction is routed through its combined plumbing.

What this could mean for insurance

All of which brings us back to my domain: the insurance industry, a space where transactions already include multiple parties, ultra-complex data structures and meticulous choices made across narrow organizational boundaries. Currently, manual underwriting, multi-step risk evaluations, document verification and legacy payment clearance are required to bind an insurance policy. But envision this paradigm in an agent-to-agent economy. Revisiting that RAV4 buyer, imagine their personal car-shopping AI agent verifying one available for purchase at a nearby dealer and then instantly contacting an insurance company’s autonomous agent. The latter examines the vehicle specs and driver history, performs underwriting computations, calculates a precise risk premium, validates data credentials, collects the premium using instant stablecoin or micro-payment rails and enacts the coverage mid-transaction – all with zero human assistance.

This is more than a hypothetical scenario. It’s an emerging reality, one that requires immediate attention from carriers and enterprise leaders. It means insurers must now develop algorithmic underwriting logic that a machine can apply and defend, construct verifiable data exchange systems that guarantee authenticity and data privacy during AI negotiations, and implement financial methods that can manage instant premium settlement 24/7. They must also begin planning for how their product gets represented, discovered, evaluated and transacted by someone else’s agent. Because the foundational infrastructure for this autonomous economy is no longer theoretical. Companies are already building the routing, identity, payment and commerce layers that could allow agents to become economic actors.

The ultimate question is not if or exactly when this machine-driven sea change will arrive. It’s what enterprises can do right now to ready their products and platforms to surf these waters successfully, catch the rising wave and ride it out with perfect poise.

item.title: IT jobs report: Employers consider AI risks and ethics
item.description:
The IT job hiring market appears to remain strong, as data from the Dice September 2026 Jobs Report shows that IT job postings continued to increase through September after experiencing a slight dip in August. Overall, the data shows that year over year, IT job postings rose 17% compared to September 2025.

Two areas that saw the most growth include AI and ML, where tech postings grew 88% in September 2026 compared to 2025, about five times faster than the average growth rate for tech postings. As employees embrace AI tools and organizations realize AI implementation goals, they’re shifting a hiring focus to security and finance roles, helping to manage and oversee emerging risks and threats as AI becomes commonplace.

With this increased focus on security and finance, organizations are realizing their AI implementation strategies. And for companies ahead of the AI curve, the focus is now on cybersecurity, governance, responsible and ethical AI use, and financial operations to support AI costs.

Skills that matter most

AI skills continue to grow in demand year-over-year and month-over-month. September saw a sharp rise in demand for Claude skills and those including agentic AI, enterprise integration, and the ethical and responsible use of AI. These skills reflect similar patterns that show in the June data, suggesting they continue to be skills consistently in demand for tech workers.

Comparing skills month-to-month, there were slight changes in demand, but electronic engineering remained the fastest growing skill since July, and skills for managing AI systems grew over September. There was also an increase in IT job postings from those looking for skills including creative problem solving, team performance management, and demonstration skills.

As AI implementation takes hold and presents new risks and challenges to IT departments across every industry, companies are also shifting focusing on cybersecurity and critical thinking skills. September saw an increase in demand for endpoint detection and prevention, as well as financial technology, indicating companies are looking for talent to manage the security and cost of AI processes and tools.

The highest growth in demand over the past year are skills involving:

  • Claude AI (1033%)
  • Agentic AI (446%)
  • Responsible AI (401%)
  • Enterprise integration (376%)
  • AI agents (308%)
  • Product family engineering (295%)
  • AI infrastructure (283%)
  • Tooling (277%)
  • Engineering practices (277%)
  • AI adoption (276%)

Month over month, the Dice report’s list of fastest growing skills includes:

  • Electronic engineering (64%)
  • Autodesk Revit (57%)
  • Endpoint detection and prevention (51%)
  • Creative problem solving (51%)
  • Database management systems (49%)
  • Team performance management (48%)
  • Data migration (45%)
  • Demonstration skills (44%)
  • FinTech (43%)

Hot hiring markets

In terms of metro areas seeing the fastest increases of job postings, not much has changed since June’s report. However the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria (DC-VA-MD-MW) area did pull ahead of New York-Newark-Jersey City (NY-NJ) metro areas, where IT job postings dipped from over 20,000 in June to just over 16,000 in September. IT job postings in metro Dallas, Chicago, and San Francisco have remained relatively unchanged since June, demonstrating potential hiring stability in these areas.

Credit: Dice September 2026 Jobs Report 

In depth:

  • AI skills are boosting IT pay — but mostly for senior roles
  • State of IT jobs: AI sparks rapidly changing market for skills
  • Facing an AI skills gap? A skills-first training approach can help
  • AI experience is the hottest IT hiring need. What if you don’t have much?

July 2026: Demand for AI fluency rises

AI skills continue to drive IT job postings, with 75% of US technology openings requiring AI fluency in June, up 178% year-over-year, according to the Dice July 2026 Jobs Report.

Roles in the software industry continue to rise, ranking second behind consulting as the industry seeking the most IT help right now. Aerospace/defense, finance/banking, and manufacturing round out the top five.

Most sought after in the market right now are software engineers, data engineers, systems engineers, electrical engineers, business analysts, data scientists, network engineers, systems administrators, data analysts, and AI engineers, according to Dice.

While these roles remain in high demand, the biggest shift can be seen in the skills that hiring managers are seeking — a list now dominated by AI or AI-adjacent skills as companies rush to adopt enterprise AI tools and services.

The skills that matter most

Demand for enterprise integration skills grew 638% from June 2025 to 2026, the biggest rise year over year, according to Dice, noting that this aligns with other indicators that “connecting agentic systems to existing infrastructure is growing faster than the agentic systems themselves.”

Following in terms of highest growth in demand over the past year are skills involving:

  • Agentic AI (587%)
  • AI agents (503%)
  • Responsible AI (495%)
  • AI infrastructure (366%)
  • Vector databases (353%)
  • Event-driven programming (310%)
  • Product family engineering (287%)
  • Prompt engineering (253%)
  • Observability (251%)

Month over month, the list of fastest growing skills in Dice’s July jobs report includes:

  • Electronic engineering (69%)
  • API system integration (58%)
  • LDAP (55%)
  • Digital forensics (54%)
  • Data exchange (53%)
  • Enterprise integration (50%)
  • Threat detection (48%)
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework (47%)
  • SAML (45%)

Again, the rise in demand for API, data exchange, and integration skills highlights the recent push to “connect AI systems to enterprise data and workflows,” according to Dice.

Hot hiring markets

Some metro areas are seeing faster increases in tech job postings, with a focus around the New York, Washington, Dallas, Chicago, and San Francisco metro areas. These areas have seen greater growth than the rest of the country, making these metro areas the best to live in if you’re a job seeker with AI fluency skills:

Credit: Dice July 2026 Jobs Report

New Jersey (64%), Maryland (47%), and Illinois (41%) are the states that have seen the highest year-over-year increase in hiring.

Roles in demand

Companies are looking for enterprise systems and consulting managers, including Appian developers, Oracle Cloud financial consultants, ServiceNow managers, principal consultants, and technology consultants. Additionally, they are seeking out IT software engineers, C++ software developers, configuration analysts, support engineers, network infrastructure engineers, AI analysts, and cyber threat intelligence analysts.

Outlook

Businesses inside and outside the tech industry will continue to seek tech workers to help realize AI visions, requiring a wide range of AI fluency and skills. It seems this trend will continue for the foreseeable future, as the job market slowly recovers from several tumultuous years.

item.title: Before you ask what an AI agent can do, ask who it is
item.description:
Companies routinely rely on authenticating the identities of humans who access sensitive company data across their networks. There’s an established and accepted set of protocols, done upfront and in a zero-trust approach – either we know who you are and let you in, or you’re locked out. The same framework needs to be applied to AI agents, posthaste.

Companies are increasingly using AI agents developed in-house, or by their vendors, partners, or clients, or, unfortunately, criminals. This can quickly add up to thousands of agents across their infrastructure and supply chains. Non-human identities outnumber human ones 45 to 1 on average in the enterprise and 144 to 1 in cloud-native environments, an increase of 44% in one year, per a recent report.

The scale and speed of this growth are beyond the ability to manually track these agents. And they have limited ability to authenticate these agents’ identities. The risks are growing. Without proper authentication, untrusted agents could access sensitive financial or customer data and share it, purposely or not, with an outside vendor, and thereby expose both the customer and the company to serious legal and compliance risk.

Many companies and security professionals are focusing on what AI agents are allowed to do in terms of permissions. But before doing that, there’s a more fundamental question they need to ask each agent: Whose agent is this? And do I trust the owner/creator? About 68% of security professionals can’t tell legitimate AI agents from malicious actors. And that question isn’t addressed at the growing scale that AI is reaching.

Email solved identity

In email, we have seen a similar story. Emails faced challenges identifying whether a sender was really who they said they were. Due to how it originated, email had no built-in authentication framework. This led to 89% of all phishing attacks having one common denominator: the sender was lying about who they were. To address this, in 2015 my cofounder and I launched a company, Valimail (valid email), to automate the emerging email authentication standard, DMARC. If I received an email claiming to be from Bank of America, DMARC checks the sender’s DNS records to authenticate whether BofA actually authorized it. Today, 100,000s of companies use the DMARC authentication standard for their inbound and outbound email.

Fast forward to today, and these ideas and patents are directly applicable to the world of AI. DMARC doesn’t rely on spotting AI-generated deception. Instead, it uses DNS as the source of truth, which is much harder to falsify.

The agent passport

With AI, we can take an analogous authentication approach. When you travel somewhere, you have a passport and a visa. The passport verifies who you are, and the visa says where you’re allowed to go/what you’re allowed to do. Similarly, today, an agent passport based on Domain Zero trust authentication can identify who the agent is (its provenance) and authorize it for the system that the agent is trying to access. Then systems can verify what an agent is allowed to do (equivalent to a visa). But first, when an agent shows up claiming to represent a vendor, the receiving system verifies its identity by checking that vendor’s DNS, applying a strict zero-trust yes/no authentication – zero ambiguity, and importantly, creating an audit trail to hold the creator accountable for any actions the Agent takes.

Given the “bad” agents outnumber “good” agents 10-100:1, a zero-trust approach focuses on the limited good/approved and the rest (near infinite bad) are rejected. Stakes are High

Without this kind of authentication, many scenarios can unfold. Almost half of employees who are using unapproved AI agents are sharing HR-related information with them and 39% transmit confidential company documents. But only 34% of organizations use the same security controls for agents as they do for human employees.

Consider this: An agent claiming to represent a third-party vendor, such as a marketing automation platform, gets access because no one confirmed it was indeed that approved vendor’s agent making the request. It accesses financial records or customer data, either downloads or modifies records, and by the time this is noticed, the damage is done.

This is a quickly moving risk. Fake invoices can appear to be authentic, and they can be generated at a scale no human fraud operation could match. Authentication used to take a phone call or a manual check. But this now has to happen instantly and automatically, at scale.

Why this matters now

Some may think email authentication is an old problem. DMARC, they say, is a decade-old fix, and the real conversation today is about AI. About 94% of organizations are dealing with increased machine identities, largely due to AI agent deployment, per Gartner, and machine identities now outnumber human accounts.

But the most common form of phishing that occurs today is when AI convincingly pretends to be someone who the target already knows and trusts. The tools for generating that deceptive attack have vastly improved. Yet the proven process for authenticating identity hasn’t kept pace, at least not for agents. This is why identity authentication is no longer optional and is now a precondition for everything else that companies want to safely do with AI agents.

What this doesn’t solve

Identity alone doesn’t solve the whole security problem. In addition, once an agent is authenticated, there are additional systems to verify what the agent is allowed to do and whether the content it produces can be trusted. Those questions come after this one. But both rely on the first one: Who is this?

Reputation

To build a reputation, you need a known identity. Once a system knows which vendor an agent represents, it can start tracking the vendor’s behavior over time and someone becomes accountable for what its agents do. And decide if the vendor should be approved and for which actions (visas). But without strong, repeatable identity authentication of agents, other security and compliance measures for agents can’t function. It’s this foundation that supports the rest of the security stack. You can’t hold an agent accountable or decide what it should be able to do until you know who it actually is. Identity is the foundation on which the rest of AI agent security must be built.

item.title: Microsoft Commits Maia to Multi-Gigawatt Inference, and Its Efficiency Metric Draws Questions
item.description:
Microsoft will scale its Maia accelerator family to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, making it the primary inference system for its own products. Maia 300 collapses scale-up and scale-out onto one Ethernet fabric and moves KV state between prefill and decode workers without leaving it. Practitioners have questioned the tokens-per-watt claim that leads the announcement.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
